A Kentucky Spiritual Guide

Recovery

Reading the Steps, working them, and the road through

This covers the Recovery section and everything it opens: the twelve steps to read, the workbook to write in, your amends list, and Recovery Road. It is the largest part of the app and the part most of it was built for.

None of this is a program. It doesn't replace a sponsor, a meeting, a treatment centre, a doctor or a pastor. It is a place to read and a place to write.

1

The Recovery menu

Tap Recovery on the home screen.

ButtonWhat's behind it
Recovery GroupsAA, NA, Personal Recovery (the steps, the workbook and Recovery Road), and your contacts. Section 2.
Recovery MeetingsMeeting finders and NA area lists for near you.
Daily ReadingsA reading for today.
Recovery BooksRecovery literature, including the Big Book.
Recovery HomesSober living and halfway houses near you.
Local SupportTreatment and support services near you.

The last three need to know roughly where you are. If you haven't set a location, the app will ask; a town or a ZIP is enough.

2

Recovery Groups

  • Alcoholics Anonymous (AA) and Narcotics Anonymous (NA) — official sites and meeting finders.
  • Personal Recovery — your own work, three doors:
    • A Kentucky Path — the steps, to read. Section 3.
    • Recovery Road — section 9. Also reachable from the Notebook menu; it's the same place either way.
    • Recovery Workbook — all twelve steps on one screen. Below.
  • Recovery Contacts — section 10.

The Recovery Workbook is a short way into the steps. Each row is one step: its number on the left, and on the right what it deals with — Honesty, Hope, Faith, and on through to Service.

  • Tap the number to read that step. It opens A Kentucky Path right on the step, without scrolling past the introduction; Back brings you to the workbook again.
  • Tap the word to write. It opens that step's own page in your workbook (section 4).
3

Reading the Steps

A Kentucky Path, subtitled From Your Porch to a Quieter Life, is the twelve steps, written plainly.

Why "for Everyone". These are written in plain language for anyone stuck on something that will not let go — a substance, a behaviour, a relationship pattern, a way of thinking. You do not have to be an addict for them to be about you.

Tap any step to read it. The Recovery Workbook's numbers (section 2) open a step here directly.

Each one has the same shape — the step itself, What This Step Means, Practical Suggestions, a Reflection to sit with, and a Prayer last. Every one of the twelve ends on a prayer — the asking comes after the looking, not before it.

At the bottom is Work Step N in my Notebook, which takes you from reading to writing. There's also Ask … about this step if you have the MASH companion app installed.

4

Working a Step

Three ways in: the button at the bottom of any step you're reading; the words in the Recovery Workbook (Recovery → Recovery Groups → Personal Recovery, section 2); or the Notebook's ☰ menu → Steps → Work, which lists all twelve and goes straight to the writing.

Most steps open a page of questions with a box under each.

There is no Save button here, and that is deliberate. Leaving the screen saves it — Back, Home, anything. Everything you typed is written on the way out. The app is built so you cannot lose work by leaving.

Return to a step later and the boxes are empty again, with a small Saved ✓ and a date where you'd written before. That's on purpose: a fresh return, with a receipt that you have been here. To read what you wrote, use What I've written →.

Four steps aren't essays and open something else instead: 4 is the inventory, 8 and 9 are the amends list in two views, and 10 is a short nightly page.

5

Step 4 — the inventory

Step 4 opens on a chooser rather than a blank page.

DoorFor
Prayers for this StepSits above the doors — prayers chosen for Step 4, not for the whole book.
Walk Me Through ItGuided, a few at a time. Section 6.
Something Good In MeSomething you did right. First on the list, always.
Something I'm Afraid OfFear — and it's the only one that ends on what you can do about it.
Someone I'm Still Mad AtResentment. Ends on the fear underneath it.
Someone I HurtHarm you've done. These become your amends list.
ShadowsThings you're not proud of where nobody else was standing there.

Why the good one is first. Step 4's own instruction is to include strengths and gifts, not only defects. An inventory that collects nothing but failures is a shame machine, and shame is the thing this app is most trying not to hand you at 2am.

Every question has a text box and a row of chips beneath it. Tapping a chip writes that word into the box — you can tap several, and you can type your own instead. Tapping a chip never deletes what you typed.

If you name more than one person in a who box, separated by commas, the app writes one row each so they reach your amends list as separate people. "Mom and Dad" written as prose stays one row.

6

Walk Me Through It

The guided version: one question at a time, and the app decides when you've done enough.

A sitting is six items — three of one kind, three of another — and then it turns: "Hey — it's getting pretty dark in here." and offers you one good question. Then That's a full sitting, with Done for now bright and One more sitting quiet.

That is there to give you a guilt-free way to stop. "I don't have one" is always offered and is always a real answer.

7

Steps 8 & 9 — the amends list

Step 8 is the list of people. Step 9 is going to them. They're one list in two views.

Anyone you named in Someone I Hurt is offered here already — you don't type them twice. Someone not in my Fourth Step adds anyone else.

Each person carries where you are with them, and you set it:

StatusMeans
Not yetOn the list. Not ready.
I'm readyReady to make it right — not that you've done it.
Not safeApproaching them would cause harm. Kept, never offered.
MadeDone.
Listed by mistakeThe name shouldn't have gone on the list. Dated like any other change, faded on the Step 8 list, and left out of Step 9's picker.

Nothing on this list can be deleted, and that is deliberate. A name you put down in error gets Listed by mistake instead — it retires the name without erasing that you wrote it. There is no delete button on Step 8, Step 9, or a person's page, and the amends list is the one thing the print screen will never clear out.

On the list itself the status is never spelled out in words. Only two of the five show at all: Made turns the name light green, and Listed by mistake fades the row. Not yet, I'm ready and Not safe look identical to anybody glancing over your shoulder.

Status changes are dated and kept, never overwritten. Moving somebody from "Not yet" to "I'm ready" two years later leaves both, with dates. The history is the point.

Step 9 opens one person at a time and asks what would make it right, whether you've talked it over with your sponsor, what you plan to do, and — afterwards — what happened.

"Not safe" people are never offered in Step 9's picker. They stay reachable from the list if you go looking, because that is a judgement at a time and not a fact about a person — but the app will not put them in front of you.

If you mark that you haven't talked it over with anyone, the app says one thing and then gets out of the way: the amends you make alone are the ones that go wrong. You can continue anyway. It is not a lock.

8

Makin' It Right

Notebook ☰ → Steps → Makin' It Right. Your amends list, laid out to be read out loud.

One person per page. Their name, where you are with them, and everything you wrote about what happened — under the words you were answering at the time. Swipe for the next one.

What this is for. Most people never hand their list to their sponsor — they read it out and explain it. This is that, on a phone, so there's no printed list to keep or lose. Use the font button, bottom right, to make it big enough to read comfortably.

Only the people you still owe appear — Not yet and I'm ready. Finished amends aren't read out, and Not safe is not in the run at all.

The page is read-only except for one thing: Talked it over — add a note at the bottom, which opens a short form for what would make it right, who you talked to, and what you plan to do. Save it and it becomes a new dated note against that person. It never overwrites the last one.

Swipe past the last person and you get Nothin' Else to Make Right. Tapping it takes you back to the Notebook.

9

Recovery Road

Thirteen places in the Bible where somebody stood where you might be standing.

They're grouped as the Wreckage, the Desert and the Rebuilding. Each door gives a place and a plain description of when you'd be there — "when strength has become strain and life is going in circles."

There is no quiz, no score, and no numbering. The app never tells you which one is yours — you'll know. And you can be at two at once. Nothing here counts how many you've read or tracks where you've been.

Each station opens part-way: At a Glance and The Story are already showing, so the page reads as something rather than a wall of buttons. Below them:

  • Your Response — three questions to sit with.
  • Recovery Connection — which Steps this connects to, with links straight into them.
  • Deep Study — the passages, the people around them, and "She stood here too" — a woman in scripture who stood in the same place.
  • Hard Questions — opens a writing page. Every box optional; not today is always a fine answer.
  • Prayers for this stretch of road — a shelf of prayers chosen for the place you're standing in, not for the whole journey.
  • If you go back out, read this first — on the Wreckage stations only. Plain words about lost tolerance: that a body which has been clean does not handle the old amount, and that this is arithmetic rather than a failing. It names how to get naloxone before it is needed, two ways, and carries the Never Use Alone line. It asks nothing of you and judges nothing.

Each station closes with a word for the road. Samson's is "The hair can grow again. It is not too late."

10

Recovery Contacts

Your call-first list: sponsor, home group, sober friends, crisis lines. Tap a number to call. Add these before you need them — the night you need this screen is not the night you want to be typing phone numbers into it.

Nearly every path through the recovery side of this app ends at a door back to this screen. That's deliberate: reading is not the last step, a person is.

11

What stays private

The recovery side holds the most private things you'll write. What the app does with them:

  • It stays on your phone, in an encrypted database. Nothing you write leaves it unless you send it — there is no account, no sync, and nowhere for it to go. The two ways it can leave are both your own doing: a backup file you make and save somewhere, and a PDF you print from Step 4. The app warns you plainly before either one.
  • Your companion cannot see most of it. Things you write about people you resent or have hurt, and your entire amends list, are refused to the AI by the app itself — whatever your sharing switch says.
  • These screens can't be screenshotted or recorded, and show blank in the app switcher. That is on purpose: the person standing next to you is a likelier problem than a hacker.
  • The app never deletes your work, and nothing is cleaned up on its own. What you can delete depends on where it is. A journal entry has a Delete on it. Step writing comes off the phone only through the one-way clear-out the print screen offers you after it has made the PDF — nothing there is ticked unless you tick it. And the amends list can't be deleted at all; see section 7.

If you write something that sounds like you might be in danger, a card appears with 988 on it. It never blocks you, never deletes what you wrote, and your words are saved the instant it appears.
